intro.title: Implement DeepPartial type
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a DeepPartial type in TypeScript, which makes all properties of an object—including nested ones—optional. You will learn the core concept of recursive type definitions, where a type references itself to handle structures of any depth. The main technologies involved are TypeScript's type system, including generics, conditional types, and mapped types. By the end, you'll understand how to create flexible, reusable types for complex data shapes, a key skill for type-safe applications.
intro.usecase: The DeepPartial type is essential when working with complex configuration objects in real-world applications. For example, in dashboard settings panels where users can customize widgets, you need to accept partial updates to deeply nested theme configurations without requiring all properties. Similarly, in content management systems, editors might update only specific fields of deeply structured article metadata while leaving other sections unchanged. This pattern also appears in API clients that send partial updates to REST endpoints, allowing selective modification of user profiles with nested address and preference objects.

objectives: Construct a DeepPartial type using conditional types and recursion
Apply the DeepPartial type to nested object structures
Implement type constraints to handle primitive values in DeepPartial
Manipulate existing type definitions to create DeepPartial variants
Integrate DeepPartial with existing TypeScript interfaces
Configure recursive type definitions for complex nested objects
Initialize type parameters for generic DeepPartial implementation

steps.title: Import TypeScript and understand the goal
steps.instruction: Create a new TypeScript file and understand that we'll be implementing a DeepPartial utility type that recursively makes all properties optional.
steps.hint: You don't need to import any libraries for this step. Just create a TypeScript file with a comment explaining the goal.
steps.seedCode:
// Create a TypeScript file for implementing DeepPartial
// DeepPartial will recursively make all properties optional
steps.expectedOutcome: A TypeScript file is created with a clear understanding of the DeepPartial type's purpose.
successCriteria: The file is a valid TypeScript file with a comment explaining the DeepPartial goal.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have a TypeScript file with a comment about implementing DeepPartial.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a TypeScript file with a comment explaining we'll implement DeepPartial to recursively make properties optional.

steps.title: Review the built-in Partial type
steps.instruction: Create a simple interface called 'User' with nested properties to demonstrate how the built-in Partial type works.
steps.hint: Define an interface with at least one nested object property, then create a variable using Partial<User> to see what becomes optional.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a User interface with nested properties and see that Partial<User> only makes top-level properties optional, not nested ones.
successCriteria: A User interface is defined with at least one nested object property, and you understand that Partial<User> doesn't affect nested properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your User interface has at least one nested object property (like an address or profile object).
steps.feedbackWrong: Create an interface named User with properties like 'name' (string) and a nested object like 'address' with its own properties.

steps.title: Define the DeepPartial type signature
steps.instruction: Define a generic type called DeepPartial<T> that will use conditional types to handle different cases. Start by writing the type declaration with a generic parameter.
steps.hint: Begin with 'type DeepPartial<T> = ' followed by your type definition. You'll expand it in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic DeepPartial<T> type is declared, ready to be implemented with conditional types.
successCriteria: The code contains a generic type named DeepPartial with a single type parameter T.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've declared a generic type named DeepPartial with a type parameter T.
steps.feedbackWrong: The DeepPartial type signature isn't defined correctly. You need to create a generic type named DeepPartial<T>.

steps.title: Handle primitive types and arrays
steps.instruction: Inside your DeepPartial type definition, add a conditional check that returns T unchanged when T is a primitive type (like string, number, boolean) or an array.
steps.hint: Use a conditional type with 'extends' to check if T is a primitive or array. You can use 'T extends (string | number | boolean | symbol | null | undefined) ? T : ...' for primitives and 'T extends Array<any> ? T : ...' for arrays.
steps.expectedOutcome: The DeepPartial type will now correctly handle primitive types and arrays by returning them unchanged instead of trying to make their properties optional.
successCriteria: The DeepPartial type includes a conditional check that returns T unchanged for primitive types (string, number, boolean, etc.) and arrays.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the conditional check might be incomplete. Make sure it handles all primitive types (string, number, boolean, symbol, null, undefined) and arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional check is missing or incorrect. Remember to use 'extends' to check if T is a primitive type or array, and return T unchanged in those cases.

steps.title: Handle object types recursively
steps.instruction: Inside the DeepPartial type definition, add a conditional branch that maps each property of an object type to DeepPartial<PropertyType> to make nested properties optional.
steps.hint: Use a mapped type with the 'in' keyword to iterate over keys of T, and apply DeepPartial to each property type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The DeepPartial type now includes a mapped type that recursively applies DeepPartial to each property of object types.
successCriteria: The DeepPartial type definition contains a mapped type using 'in keyof T' that applies DeepPartial to each property type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct syntax for mapped types and applying DeepPartial recursively.
steps.feedbackWrong: The mapped type for handling object properties recursively is missing or incorrect. Review how to create mapped types in TypeScript.

steps.title: Add the final DeepPartial implementation
steps.instruction: Complete the DeepPartial<T> type by writing the full implementation that handles primitives, arrays, and objects recursively.
steps.hint: Use a conditional type to check if T extends primitive types or arrays, then use a mapped type for objects with recursive DeepPartial application.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: complete conditional type implementation
type OptionalAll<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: OptionalAll<T[K]> } : T;
steps.expectedOutcome: The DeepPartial type should be fully implemented with proper conditional logic and recursive mapping.
successCriteria: DeepPartial<T> correctly handles primitive types, arrays, and objects with recursive optional properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if your implementation correctly handles all three cases: primitives, arrays, and objects recursively.
steps.feedbackWrong: The implementation doesn't match the expected structure. Review how conditional types and mapped types work together for recursive optional properties.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Compare with built-in Partial
steps.instruction: Create a final example that demonstrates the difference between Partial and DeepPartial by applying both to a nested object type and logging the results.
steps.hint: Define a nested object type, create variables using both Partial and DeepPartial, and use console.log to show that DeepPartial makes all nested properties optional while Partial only affects top-level.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will see that DeepPartial allows optional nested properties while Partial only makes top-level properties optional.
